item.title: From aero pockets made on a dining table to skinsuits worn by Mark Cavendish – How one rider took Nopinz from Devon to a world-leading 'everyday aero' brand
item.author: Andy McGrath
item.content:encoded: A couple of thousand years before bike racing even existed, Plato had it right: necessity is the mother of all invention. An elite racer in the UK finishing at the sharp end of the country’s time trials on highways and byways, Blake Pond was getting into an unwanted routine. He would lovingly spend several minutes getting his race number pinned perfectly for every time trial. It was a need, driven by aesthetics, aerodynamics and fastidiousness.When he jumped on the bike, rode off and heard a ripping noise, he knew what it meant: gigantic pinholes in a speed suit which had cost a week of his bike shop mechanic wages. The alternative fate was just as undesirable: he would pass riders with numbers flapping like parachutes. "On the drive back, I was thinking there’s got to be a better way of doing this," Pond tells over coffee.His solution: a stretchy pocket, as you’d find on a documents-enclosed envelope, stuck on a skinsuit with special adhesive. Initially, the idea went in his training kit drawer for a few years, doubting its mass appeal. But he was drawn back to it after hearing other racers airing their frustration or even yelps of pain from competitors accidentally getting stuck by a pin-wielding friend trying to give them perfectly flat race numbers.In 2014, Nopinz was born with the SpeedPocket. At first, it was just Pond, his computer and a heat press. The next iteration involved using a seamstress to sew in this aero addition before posting the garment back. In little more than a decade, his company has gone from the dining room table in the Devon town of Bideford in the south-west of the United Kingdom and a self-explanatory brand name to more than 50,000 orders and the WorldTour, with a range of apparel and aerodynamic accessories tailored for TT, road racing, triathlon, running and indoor cycling. The WorldTour teams and riders supported along the way include Mark Cavendish on his record-breaking 'Project 35' stage-win quest at the Tour de France.Nopinz wouldn't be where it is today without the community’s explosion of interest in aero gains over the last decade. "How optimised everyone’s got in TT is crazy. When I was racing back in 2014, I had a lot of watts but not a lot of aero," Pond reflects. "And now it’s shifted the other way completely. I’m going the same sort of speed as I was back then, off 15 per cent less power."An aero obsessive, Pond climbed a lamppost at the 2015 Tour de France prologue in Utrecht to take photographs of riders from above. This obsession feeds their comprehensiveness, testing products in the wind tunnel at Silverstone, prototyping in-house and doing fabric tests. WorldTour recognition for 'everyday aero' kit"We always test and market the averages. If we test at 40, 45 and 50 [km/h] and nought to seven degrees of yaw, we’ll average it out across the speeds we’re aiming that product at," he says, implying that they do not cherry-pick certain data for marketing. Alongside the weighted model designed to better reflect real-world riding conditions that he mentions, theirs is a competitive price point: their popular Sonic socks cost £24.99.Pond has tried to keep their pricing reasonable, though he is aware of the perverse "reassuringly expensive" philosophy that can pervade in the sport. More expensive does not necessarily mean better. "We need to make the margin in the suit and obviously get profit out of it, but it comes to a stage where you’re making it up, really. Sometimes that does happen with other brands – I can’t understand why the suits are so pricey when we can do it [for cheaper] and do all the R&D," he says.For the founder, Nopinz suits are for the person who can’t spend £20,000 in a wind tunnel. "Maybe we’re doing it more cost-effectively. There’s a ceiling price: we want to be that reliable sort of partner: you know you’re getting a really good product and it’s not stupidly expensive. That’s how I see it really: NoPinz – everyday aero."As the framed and signed jerseys around their HQ in the Devon town of Barnstaple attest, the WorldTour wanted a piece of their watt savers too. Starting with support for LottoJumbo-NL in 2015, riders from the likes of FDJ, Israel-Premier Tech and AG2R have all benefited. Alex Dowsett bought his own skinsuits from the company and wore one to win a 2020 Giro d’Italia stage.The company became an official TT partner to WorldTour team Intermarché the next season, giving it visible "additional credibility" after years of secretly supplying ingredients to the bunch, without recognition or under an NDA. Pond says Nopinz was offered a full clothing partnership with the Belgian squad but couldn't accommodate the approximate £500,000 outlay, nor the quantity of kit. "That sort of commitment would be crushing," he says.Still, teams or riders came calling with projects – and you might be surprised at how disorganised and last-minute pro cycling can be. One of the company’s latest nights on the job involved working with takeaway boxes after Israel-Premier Tech realised several days before the Tour de France start that they had sent the wrong designs for their special edition skinsuits. One of their coaching team drove from the south of France to Devon, got a few hours’ kip in Pond’s campervan while Nopinz put on a production run of 50 suits, turning it around in 24 hours in time for him to drive to the Grand Départ. Cutting-edge materials and UCI pushback There is a knick-knack sign in Pond’s home which says 'One bike ride away from a good mood'. He was inspired to get in the saddle by hearing tales of the sport: his grandfather, Lew Pond, was a rival of British track sprint icon Reg Harris and was selected for the 1948 Olympics in tandem racing. After starting in triathlons, he moved to the family’s legacy sport and quickly noticed his bike leg was his strongest. Becoming an elite-licensed racer, he finished seventh in the British national TT championships, although being knocked off by a car led to a back injury which stopped competition between 2014 and 2024. Now back pinning on numbers using his own SpeedPocket – and winning time trials galore in the UK’s south-west – being in the racing environment helps him to understand his customer base and generate ideas.Pond regards himself as a "fake CEO" and more a hands-on, jack of all trades, doing everything from business direction, budgeting, R&D, product design and social media to fixing machines, using his old bike mechanic nous. Reinvestment in his company has often been preferable to status symbols: when he had the money to consider buying himself a Porsche, a new laser cutter for Nopinz took priority.Investing in the cutting-edge was worthwhile for their latest skinsuit, the Hypersonic Mk2, building on their original, double-layered (base layer and skinsuit) aero iteration. "We dared to be a bit different with it," he says.Top speed-suits use a lot of the similar striped fabric on the sleeves, which he dubs 'Super Stripe'. Pond and Nopinz collectively spent four years looking for an aero, textured fabric that would be faster. A year and a half ago, he found his Eureka material from a company on Italy’s Lake Como and christened it Speedcell. It wasn’t cheap, coming in at roughly £45 a metre at orders of 250 metres minimum, but worth every penny. From a rudimentary aero test, switching from the former material to the new one, the basic prototype showed measurable gains, and they made improvements to the fit. It looks different – sci-fi, even – it feels different, and their testing proved that it saved watts.An ongoing challenge for Pond is keeping up with UCI regulations. In 2022, the sport’s governing body banned the SpeedPocket at mass events after a consultation with a working group of manufacturers. It was a bitter pill to swallow. "Brands started to cotton on to it and were doing their own versions, but the trouble was, you could hardly see the numbers," he says. Economic challenges, sustainability, and 'Project 35'Governing body caprices are just one blast in the face for a business that has faced "one headwind after another" in the last five years.The vast majority of the cycling industry can relate. He estimates raw fabric costs have risen "15 to 20" per cent, likely due to the increasing cost of oil and the raw materials used. War has a knock-on effect, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict causing a spike in prices.Shipping costs have also risen considerably, and Brexit added complications. While Pond produces in the UK, fabrics are bought from European nations or ones outside the continent, bringing pressures associated with import and export."Because the industry has been so negative and there’s been so much discounting, you can’t pass it on or win it back," he adds.From Nopinz’s side, wage inflation and increased National Insurance contributions have added approximately £90,000 to their wage bill across a team of 15, which has been streamlined in recent years. It all means the customer feels the pinch. A European client will have to pay VAT and additional tariffs as well as possible fuel charges and surcharges from delivery operators, even though Nopinz do customs duties and taxes paid now (i.e. settled by the sender) to try to mitigate nasty surprises. With all the added costs, a would-be buyer might easily abandon their shopping basket and drop off. "That’s been quite hard to navigate," Pond says.It has become harder to manufacture in the UK and make a profit. Nopinz has been flat in terms of growth in recent years, but making a profit, which he perceives to be rare. "We’d obviously love to see Nopinz go back on that growth trajectory, but we don’t want to do it at the expense of being a sustainable business," he says. In a crowded market of apparel makers at similar price points, Pond expects they will focus more on the high-end side of the sport and the pinnacle. "I feel that’s where we can differentiate ourselves as a brand," he says."We want to have products that people go ‘I’m racing, this is super important, I’ve trained really hard, and I want to make sure I invest in the kit.’ We want them to think Nopinz when it comes to cycling products.""Being small is good. We’ve got the Speedcell now, and we’re already looking for the next thing – we’ve acknowledged we’ve done that, now someone else is going to do that, and the only way we can stay one step in front is being able to rapidly prototype and produce something," Pond says."In a company with a lot more management and structure, it might take two years for a product to be conceived and actually find its way to market. Whereas for us, it can be 10 days if we have to, like something to do with Cavendish."Ah yes, collaborating with the greatest sprinter in the sport. As office dogs Rodney and Cassandra pad in and out of the HQ boardroom to the whirr of air compressors, Pond locates a pair of surprisingly small white shoes with a blue Nike tick which belonged to the sprinter extraordinaire. Yes, Nopinz was part of 'Project 35'. Nopinz brand ambassador Alex Dowsett, a fellow aero geek, went to the wind tunnel with Cavendish in the middle of 2024 and called Pond, wanting to fine-tune every possible aero gain in his pursuit of the record.Turning round prototypes and testing them at Silverstone rapidly, Nopinz worked up toe overshoes ('Hypersonic Tovershoes') and eye-catching textured, shoelace covers. "We tried to simulate the texture of the laces, while also tidying up the aero around the Boa [dial]," he says. There was also what would become the Hypersonic Mk2 socks, initially called P35, with V-shaped aero chevrons. However, Pond was mindful that, due to UCI equipment rules, anything used for competition has to be on the market. "I said ‘put them on [the website] for £1,000 so nobody buys them’ – and somebody did," he says.Nopinz also contributed a road race suit for lead-out man Michael Mørkøv and Cavendish. Optimised for hotter conditions using graphene, according to Pond, the Manxman rode it for the sweltering first day across Italy, where he was nearly eliminated in the time cut. "Unfortunately for us, just not on the stage he won," Pond adds. "But it was super cool to be involved and asked at the eleventh hour, and have someone of Mark’s level and standing. He did ride most of that Tour in our stuff."Whether it is for road racing’s greatest fast man or the rider looking to win the town sign sprint on the club ride, Pond is constantly thinking about how to get ahead of the competition with his 'everyday aero' apparel. So, what is the future of high-performance clothing in racing? He imagines fabrics that adjust their own textures to different speeds in the real world. "There are already fabrics that can control how they react electronically, so you can imagine that with a speed suit or something where the texture changes as they go from 30km/h to 50km/h. Optimising itself as you’re riding." He likens them to people in Tron-style suits, a bit like when Nike did Back to the Future auto-closing shoes. Good luck getting that one past the UCI.

item.title: Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings
item.author: Cyrus Farivar
item.content:encoded: Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal" in Florida.

item.title: MLB, college sports, and the sports propaganda moment
item.author: John Griffin
item.content:encoded: When we’re in school, we hear a lot about propaganda. American history textbooks show us political cartoons from the late 19th and early 20th century about the abolition of slavery, the rise of industrial robber-barons, and the progressive movement. European art historians discuss how Louis XIV used paintings and sculptures to present himself as the “Sun King” as he strengthened the power of the French crown over the First and Second Estates. In my own Roman history classes, I spend multiple weeks demonstrating how the emperors employed literature, history, sculpture, and construction projects to assert the supremacy of both Rome and the imperial household. Whether in middle school, high school, or college, students regularly grapple with propaganda in their history classes, learning how people with access to communicative resources have been able to present their own version of reality to sway public opinion in their favor.Once we’re out of school, though, propaganda falls by the wayside, and ceases to be a concern. It exists, in the public consciousness at least, not as a part of our lives, but as a historical oddity, the behavior of a bygone era — or, when it’s acknowledged in the modern world, as something that happens in the nebulous “over there,” not “here.” And yet, what else can we call the flood of political advertisements in every commercial break that made the World Series borderline unwatchable if not propaganda? After all, are they not trying to sell their version of reality, as opposed to that of their opponents, in an effort to sway voters?Propaganda is most often understood in terms of politics, but it doesn’t have to be. And right now, we’re living in what I call a sports propaganda moment, as two major entities — the NCAA and Major League Baseball — have gone on the figurative warpath, spending millions of dollars in advertising not to get people to watch their product, but to generate outrage from fans on their own behalf against that of their players. Whether you’re a fan of a power conference school who competes for the national championship every year or a small liberal arts college who celebrates when their team gets blown out during the March Madness tournament because that meant they made it in the first place, you’ve almost certainly been exposed to commercials sponsored by the Saving College Sports organization in support of the Protect College Sports Act. Since the start of the 2026 college football season (and in truth, since last bowl season, as commercials in support of the bill ran even before it was officially introduced in Congress back in June), they have run a massive ad campaign encouraging fans to contact their congressional representatives and pressure them to vote yes on the bill. Backed by multi-million athletic programs and employing household names such as Deion Sanders and Nick Saban (a current coach and a former one, respectively), these ads center the conversation about the bill on the legitimate concerns fans have about today’s Wild West NIL era — namely, the constant transfers — while ignoring the fact that the bill attempts to, as much as legally possible, reassert the extreme levels of control that the conferences and schools used to have over their athletes.Starting in the middle of the summer, Major League Baseball has rolled out their own ad campaign in preparation for the upcoming lockout, which is now just a week and a half away. Focused on MLB.tv and social media, the “Level the Playing Field” campaign directly argues for the implementation of a salary cap and floor, claiming that the league cannot have competitive balance due to the payroll disparities that exist between small- and large-market teams. These ads ran all summer, during the All-Star Game festivities, the postseason, the World Series, and the awards season. While, ironically, this meant that the league plastered everywhere a chart in which the team with the second-highest payroll, the Mets, missed the playoffs as the team with the second-lowest payroll, the Rays, won the pennant, the very fact that the league spent time and energy publicly fighting the players during what should be the biggest annual celebrations of the sport is a testament to their priorities — and the important role that these ads played in their pre-lockout preparations.Now, obviously, these two situations aren’t 100 percent comparable. Decades of corruption and a refusal to negotiate common sense solutions with its players forced college athletes to turn to the courts for assistance, and once the courts got involved, federal involvement and oversight was all but guaranteed, and all the political machinations that entails. Major League Baseball, meanwhile, is attempting, for the second time this decade, to use the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement as an opportunity to break the power of the players’ union and implement the salary cap that they believe will see franchise values skyrocket. Sure, the almighty dollar may be the driving force for both the NCAA and MLB — both the Protect College Sports Act and the salary cap are, at their core, attempts to rein payrolls in and ensure cost certainty — but each organization is so fundamentally different from the other that their financial systems are incomparable. Nonetheless, the fact that both collegiate athletics and professional baseball have adopted the same tactic, large-scale propaganda campaigns meant to turn the fans against the players, reflects the unique historical moment we are in. As we saw during the last CBA negotiations, social media has allowed players to interact with fans directly, allowing them to, for example, directly argue against the league’s propaganda, much like Jameson Taillon did last week.Last time around, this direct connection between players and fans appeared to help the players in the negotiations, as the players were able to successfully mock the league’s insistence on removing all evidence of players’ likenesses on all media. That being said, should there be a disconnect between the fans and the players, this has the potential to backfire on the players, and perhaps this is what Major League Baseball is going for here. Baseball may be in the midst of a renaissance, but that doesn’t mean the fans don’t think that some things need to be fixed. Deferred money, especially when done to the extent the Dodgers have in recent years, has been regularly mocked in baseball-related online spaces. The rise of gambling has resulted in real, concrete ethics concerns. Blackouts, TV restrictions, and an ever-increasing stable of required streaming services have made watching the games a veritable chore. Solving none of these problems requires a salary cap, and yet, the league has tried to use their media machine to tie all of them to it, to limited success. In fact, it may have backfired just a bit: the frequency with which they have said “this proposal is contingent on the players accepting a salary cap” has sparked quite a bit of mockery online.Of course, what has sparked such a large push for a cap at this time is the fact that this CBA negotiation might be the league’s best guaranteed opportunity for one in the foreseeable future. The Dodgers and the Mets have giftwrapped the league two bogeymen to use to sway fans to their side in the negotiations: between the former’s willingness to exploit deferred money and their acquisitions of Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Rōki Sasaki, Blake Snell, Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Tyler Glasnow, Teoscar Hernández, and Tarik Skubal over the last three years, and the latter’s willingness to ignore all luxury tax thresholds and common sense to sign whatever hot free agents they can, there’s quite a bit of ammunition to turn fans of small- and medium-market teams against the owners. The Players’ Association, meanwhile, has been in a bit of disarray this year, with Tony Clark one of several union executives shown the door within the last 12 months; while it’s unclear whether this will actually harm the union in negotiations, turmoil at the top can at least give the impression of weakness to an ownership group looking to make major gains. Together, these scenarios have things ripe for Major League Baseball to push all their chips to the center of the table and try to get their salary cap, as it might be their best opportunity for a while. And so, the propaganda machine spins on.

item.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
item.author: Mark Sweney
item.content:encoded: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergenciesThe Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.Continue reading...

item.title: 'There is certainly no bitterness' – Case against truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin won't continue due to his ill health
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The hearings into the case of Wolfgang Rieke, the truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin, have concluded with no charges brought.Two years ago, a first-instance trial concluded with Rieke being sentenced to a four-year jail term after hitting and killing Rebellin in 2022. However, the Venice Court of Appeals ruled last week that Rieke is unfit to participate in an appeal trial, so the case has been dropped, according to the news agency.Rieke, 66, currently resides in a nursing home after suffering a stroke in 2024, and this summer his lawyers obtained a doctor's report on his psychological and physical ability to participate in the trial. The report concluded that Rieke is mentally unable to stand trial."The family acknowledges what happened. There is certainly respect for the judicial decisions and today's. There is certainly no bitterness; there is acknowledgement and respect for his health," said Rebellin's family's lawyer, Davide Picco."Justice has certainly worked, given that the Prosecutor's Office transferred the defendant from Germany to Italy. He served several months in prison and then under house arrest. His health condition then led to today's sentence."Rieke, who had previously pled guilty to a non-fatal hit-and-run and drunk driving, struck and killed Rebellin as he was on a training ride in Montebello Vincentino on November 30, 2022, shortly after he retired from racing. He then fled the scene, leading authorities to launch a multi-country search.He turned himself in to German police in June 2023 and was later handed a four-year sentence after the judge rejected several initial plea deals. After suffering a stroke two years ago, the case against him will not continue."We are satisfied that the judges have accepted our requests, acknowledging Mr. Rieke's current health conditions, which prevent him from consciously participating in the trial," said Rieke's lawyer, Andrea Nardin, according to the Corriere del Veneto.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Science has a home here at Ars—please help keep it that way
item.author: John Timmer
item.content:encoded: It's now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I've known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It's no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I'd like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I'm unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars' future through your support will mean I don't have to.But I'd rather make a case for why you'll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I'll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

item.title: Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: “3 straight on the road, what’s up…”
item.author: Moritz Wollert
item.content:encoded: LaMelo Ball hit one of his patented three-pointers from the left elbow early in the third quarter against the New York Knicks last night and as the crowd cheered, he proceeded to jog back on defense. Of course, the only not totally broken Ball brother couldn’t let the moment pass without completely indulging himself into a thoroughly scripted “ice in the veins”-gesture that feels as original these days as a two-handed set shot. Just a moment later Josh Hart rained on the parade, running directly by Vanilla Ball’s D and finishing an easy backdoor cut with a simple layup. And just like that the Knicks were up 14 again, ignoring the protocol of how cutting a deficit to 12 in a game where your team got handsomely dominated up to that point needs to be celebrated.It feels good to root for a professional team, doesn’t it? It will allow you to say things like Real Clydes Wear Plaid shared in the and which I unapologetically stole for the headline of this recap. The Knicks won their third game in a row at Minnesota last night and they probably made it a lot harder than it needed to be. Their opponents certainly had something to do with it, no matter how ill-advised some individual emotions might have been. The Timberwolves can play tremendous defense, are as long as those trees in their logo and have an aggression you could certainly link to that name-giving animal of them. They got a good albeit cranky coach, a proven system, years of winning experience. Yet in the end they also got LaMelo Ball now.Knicks hold off Minnesota’s late rallyWe get that he is a talented, at times iconic passer; we also get that he has found his footing fairly well on the frozen tundra near the Great Lakes so far. But we really can’t get convinced that you can ever really win big with a “talent” like that. His play can remind one of the game young kids play before they really get a hang of Dr. Naismith’s rules. They also take two steps before every dribble, then four after they pick the ball up. They also couldn’t care less about a repetitive shooting motion or dribbling the ball without palming it every time. With the kids it’s okay and fun, we let them discover themselves as players and excuse it. But Lamborghini LaMelo should be held to a different standard, he is supposed to be a professional NBA player after all.Luckily for the Knicks, they got plenty of real pros on their roster, guys who truly care about winning and treat their profession like it means something – not only to them but to others. It certainly seemed that way when they played most of the game last night with a level of calmness and concentration that has been a hallmark of theirs ever since they went on that beautiful championship run last year. But despite all their dominance over that two-month stretch in the playoffs, you can’t ignore that they are a team with plenty of cracks in their armor, many of which showed themselves last night as well. It’s the kind of weakness that are often the reason for the Bockers falling behind big only to have the opportunity to stage their beloved monumental comebacks later on.Knicks’ defense wins it in the endYesterday the Knicks offense completely bogged down late when Minnesota went to more switching on D (raise your hand if you’ve seen that before), neutralizing all the beautiful team basketball that helped the Gotham Gang run up an almost 20-point lead earlier. Not even Karl-Anthony Towns, once again mesmerizing for most of the night against a traditional five at his old stomping grounds, couldn’t regain his first-half form. Maybe he rode the pine a little long, Mr. Brown? Well, you can’t play him all 48, we get it. A lineup that included Jose Alvarado, Andre Drummond and Josh Hart was still an interesting choice, to say the least. For all the individual chops it’s quite a load for Jalen Brunson to carry that group offensively, it almost feels like him heaving big AD up K2 or some other majestic mountain. It might get you to the summit against certain defenses but considering some defenses are as long and physical as the Wolf Pack, it can also get cold rather quickly. Especially when Brunson still hasn’t found his touch inside the paint yet.That New York could still pull it out in the end is a testament to timely plays and a gritty, opportunistic defense that at no point in the game relented to the physically imposing Wolves coming at them. When LaMelo Ball couldn’t find someone open downtown, the canines’ only plan was to ram their oversized combo forwards ahead. It worked here or there but never consistently. Watch out, there’s an extended arm coming at you – boom, another offensive foul! It’s an interesting yet understandable choice by the league to make the off arm a point of emphasis this year (sorry, SGA). Why didn’t they do the same for palming the basketball or taking more steps than a dressage horse? Your guess is as good as mine.For the moment, though, let us not worry about it – there is a win to be celebrated. For all we know though, our guys are probably watching some film right now and preparing for their next opponent (Portland on Saturday). Maybe they are also speeding race cars through some busy pedestrian zone or practice their one-legged step-back fadeaway jumper that has netted them less than 42 percent shooting for their career?Nah, we leave that to the guy with ice in his veins.

item.title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
item.author: Jon Brodkin
item.content:encoded: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption.The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

item.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalismIt’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.Continue reading...

item.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
item.author: Henrietta Moore
item.content:encoded: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workersAI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programmeContinue reading...

If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.Continue reading...

item.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 11/20/26
item.author: Madison Pavich
item.content:encoded: We’re less than a week away from Thanksgiving now, and the Yankees have started to get a bit active before the holidays kick in. After locking down David Bednar’s contract for 2027, there were overnight musings that Jonathan Loáisiga reportedly is coming back to New York after a year away in Arizona. His 2026 season was excellent, and it was also the first healthy season he’d had in a while, but up until now it seemed like there was more interest from the Dodgers or Mets than the Yankees. If they managed to get a hometown discount for their former reliever then they might’ve gotten away with a bit of a steal, but we’ll have to wait and see what the actual details of this potential deal are. We’ve got a few things in store for you today, beginning with John giving us his thoughts on MLB’s early PR propaganda laying the ground for their side of the upcoming lockout. Jonathan hands out our latest report card to the rookie George Lombard Jr. after his whirlwind second half with the big league team, Kevin remembers the legacy of one of baseball’s early titans in Clark Griffith, and then in the afternoon I’ll be back to answer your latest mailbag questions. 1. If the Yankees have Jonathan Loáisiga back in the fold, how many games do you expect to see him in next year? 2. Do they still need another established reliever in your mind, or do you trust Brian Cashman and Matt Blake to make due from here?

item.title: Why a 37-year-old Primož Roglič is still a great signing and how more freedom at NSN can unlock his five-time Grand Tour-winning best
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: The further into the off-season it went, the more likely it seemed that five-time Grand Tour winner Primož Roglič's career was going to end before he wanted it to. It wasn't like most of the big-name moves in modern cycling, which are signposted months in advance, but it did finally bring an answer to the question that Roglič had been answering with "We'll see, ah" and "I don't know yet" ever since July, when Red Bull team boss Ralph Denk confirmed he would be leaving. The idiosyncrasies that have made him one of the peloton's most popular and compelling riders won't be going anywhere, instead just repackaged in the Swiss team's colours for, as they described it, the "final chapter".Though it should be noted that Roglič hasn't ruled out a similarly complicated re-up of his time in the sport 12 months from now, more openly putting it down to needing "some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never."Tudor, Pinarello Q36.5, Unibet Rose Rockets, and XDS Astana were among the other speculated landing spots for the Slovenian, but clearly none could muster up the perfect mix of financial resources, a fitting contract, or the desire to bring him in, but NSN have found room for the GC star.Importantly, it means that instead of a nondescript 68th-place finish at Il Lombardia, 37-year-old Roglič is now in control of where his final chapter as a professional comes to an end, and he certainly won't be looking to go out with a whimper. "I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself," he said, when his surprise move to NSN was announced on Wednesday evening. "I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."After his home heroics in Slovenia late in the season, Roglič will start his 12th year in the WorldTour as the reigning European time trial champion, which he wasn't even sure he'd get to wear in a race after he won it: "Maybe I'll only wear it at home. Because we haven't decided yet what I'll do next, but no matter what, I'll wear it."Off the bike for 10 days and unsure if he would have even taken the start if it wasn't where he lived, Roglič's late-season results should be looked at with the context that what he did was nothing short of miraculous when it came to recovery. This is far from the sort of moves that saw the then Israel-Premier Tech – which was rebranded as NSN a year ago – criticised as something of a "retirement home". Roglič may be a veteran, but he is still one of the top riders in the world.Roglič raced 53 times in 2026, with mixed success, but importantly, still with success. He opened up his campaign with a solid performance at Tirreno-Adriatico, finishing fifth overall and helping teammate Giulio Pellizzari to third on GC behind winner Isaac del Toro, and followed that up with more success in Italy by taking third at Milano-Torino. From here, things slowed down for the Slovenian, finishing 16th at Iztulia Basque Country, and failing to impress at the Tours de Romandie and Suisse as compatriot Tadej Pogačar dominated the racing to take both titles. Roglič only managed 18th and eighth overall, respectively.He turned things around at the Slovenian national championships, ramping up his performance with a win in the ITT and fourth in the road race, ahead of his already confirmed major goal of the Vuelta, where he was looking to stand alone at the top of the history books for the most overall titles – which he currently shares alongside Roberto Heras on four. However, it was soon after, on July 31, that Roglič revealed he had been halted in his plans: "Got hit by a car few days ago…" read a post on his Instagram. "I won't be participating in San Sebastian and in Burgos unfortunately... not the best scenario, but it's life, eh. Now it's all systems go towards La Vuelta; we work and hope things will turn around!"He did make it to the Vuelta, and while there were no of old – as it was Enric Mas who stepped into the spotlight and claimed red after Pogačar crashed out – when all was said and done in Granada, Roglič could only describe second as feeling "like a victory to me".Mas rightly took the majority of headlines as he made history for Spain, but there was a more visceral reaction from the press room as second-place Roglič answered his final question in the longer post-race press conferences. It felt like a goodbye to the race where he had enjoyed his most successful moments, with no one in the room, nor he, knowing where he'd end up next as the room filled with applause and matching gratitude from the Slovenian.The same feelings returned at European Championships and Il Lombardia, where the enigmatic Roglič was none the wiser, still saying, "You never know when is the last one. Like everything in life, it can be a bit emotional," as he conceded that the Italian Monument could be the endpoint.Into the off-season, Roglič next resurfaced at the Taiwan Cycling Masters, where a KOM challenge south of Taipei saw the Slovenian drop no hints at whether he'd signed a contract – instead, he continued to be cryptic in his comments. "The people that you collect on the way, or they collect you, that you have around, they help the influence at the end on you," he said in a promotional video for the event. "I think yes, they left a mark on me, like I said I'm always open to learn, to know more, and the more you know, the more you know that you don't know, so it's a never-ending process."Well now we do know, as does he, that life in the pro peloton will be continuing, and while those previously ruthless punchy legs perhaps lack the same bite they had five-eight years ago, he has a diesel engine that can still power him up the highest mountains. In his best results at the Europeans and Vuelta, it's key not to forget that it wasn't against weak fields by any means; at the former, Bruno Armirail, Stefan Küng, and Jakob Söderqvist were among those unable to live with Roglič's time, and at the latter he emerged ahead of Giro runner-up Felix Gall, new teammate Richard Carapaz, and Oscar Onley for his second place on GC. How he could fit into NSN's plansEven with Roglič clearly proving his worth as an asset into his late 30s, there still remains the question of how NSN will deploy their new leader and fit him into their schedules after such a late pick-up. The team's media day is next week, and the thoughts will already be on December and January training camp ahead of the start of the 2027 season on January 1, with rider schedules among the news set to be confirmed in the coming weeks. With Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt, NSN had already been looking to improve their stock as a GC-hunting outfit, having failed to finish in the top 10 of all three Grand Tours in 2026. Their best results were 12th at the Giro, 68th at the Tour, and 15th at the Vuelta, but with those three mentioned above and Roglič, they suddenly have a chance at finishing in the top 10 and potentially higher of all three. Carapaz has already suggested that it is a return to the Giro where he wants to target an overall placing, and while this would seem to interfere with a potential Slovenian homecoming for Roglič, it's actually the Tour and Vuelta that look like more likely targets. Sharing the leadership among their new star signings lessens any chance for internal bickering, and also opens the door to Carapaz potentially chasing GC at one Grand Tour and then stages and the mountains classification at another – as he'd been doing successfully for EF in recent years. NSN's new foray into the GC hierarchy also represents more freedom for a rider like Roglič, who has been bitten by bad luck and crashes several times in the most pressure-filled moments riding for Visma and Red Bull – teams where you to maintain GC success to keep your spot.Roglič should get the freedom to pick the plan which suits him best and allows him to build up in the ways he knows will work for GT success. NSN will also offer up what Red Bull didn't in his final Vuelta for them this past summer, where a young team lacking in climbing support saw them struggle to front up numbers to muster a major challenge consistently against Mas – even if it likely would have had no effect on the final red jersey standings. NSN can commit their younger riders Buitrago and Van Eetvelt, and the experience of George Bennett and Nick Schultz to a full-blown Roglič bid, be that at the Tour or Vuelta. And while in an age of Pogačar, Vingegaard, Evenepoel, Seixas, and Del Toro, any entrance into the top-five seems unlikely, this summer proved that anything can happen, even to the big stars, with Pogačar crashing out of the Vuelta and Vingegaard from the Tour, so it's not out of the realms of possibility that he is able to score one final Grand Tour podium, which would be his 10th, or indeed a sixth victory.In reality, Roglič's goals could become a final stage win at the Tour – to add to the three he already has, 10 years after his first into Serre-Chevalier on stage 17 of the 2017 race – the GC title at the Tour de Suisse, which remains the only major one-week stage race missing from his palmarès from the seven, or indeed that elusive fifth Vuelta title. Even with Pogačar probably taking the start, living by the words "Never say never" has got Roglič this far, and he'll be hoping his new team's name can carry him to the last hurrah which he deserves. There's a degree of risk in not allowing that European title win on home roads to become the denouement to his great career, but as one Slovenian famously said en route to one of his Vuelta titles: "No risk, no glory." item.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
item.author: Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk
item.content:encoded: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recordedMultiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.Continue reading...

item.title: Cadillac ditches plan to produce own V6 hybrid engine ahead of F1’s V8 push
Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: Scenes from a beautiful game with a funky tail
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: The Timberwolves (11-5) have been the talk of the West, especially with their level of success given the absence of star guard Anthony Edwards (knee). Coach Chris Finch has his crew chucking up 116.7 points per game while also leading the league in rebounding and fielding the top defense. So far this season, the Wolves have held every opponent to under 50% from the floor—and they would again tonight. New York (9-6) knew the trouble that awaited them as they squared off with their first Western Conference team of the season. The game started with runs in either direction, but the Knicks gained steam and took a 15-point lead into halftime. In the third quarter, Minnesota chipped away at the lead, and Jaden McDaniels led the doggies on a rally in the fourth quarter to cut the lead to three with a scant few minutes left. But neither team could buy a bucket down the stretch. The Knicks went scoreless for the final three and a half minutes, the T’Wolves missed on everything, and the visitors escaped with a 102-99 victory.That’s the lowest score for the Wolves this season. Take a bow, fellas.On a first-quarter drive, LaMelo Ball (your favorite Ball brother?) swiped an arm across Jalen Brunson’s face. Cap was rattled by it and subbed out around the nine-minute mark, giving Tyler Kolek an unusually early appearance. With Jalen out, the visitors went on a 12-0 run. The backup guard was terrific in his first-half play, dishing five dimes in seven minutes, a third of the team’s total, and leading a second unit that tallied 17 first-half points.A game of runs! Minny responded with a 13-2 run that included Ball attacking the paint for points and Jaden McDaniels swishing from long range. McDaniels was Minnesota’s most efficient scorer in the half, putting up 11 points on perfect 4-of-4 shooting, including three triples (but also three costly turnovers). Returning the favor, Josh Hart dropped a triple that started an 11-3 run and gave New York a 33-26 lead at the break.In the second quarter, KAT and OG Anunoby stepped further into the spotlight. They combined for 30 first-half points on 12-of-18 shooting. Karl sang beautifully on his former home court, scoring 17 points and hauling in eight boards in just 16 minutes; OG chimed in with 13 points and a pair of blocks. Jose Alvarado got a little run but was quiet in the quarter. In a nice return to form, Josh Hart added nine points on 3-of-4 shooting from deep, while steady-eddie Landry Shamet provided a major lift off the bench with 10 points and a team-best plus-17 in 17 minutes.The T’Wolves have length that can really clog the lane, and that explains why Jalen Brunson managed just seven points on 2-of-8 shooting, with his two makes coming from the outfield. Against most teams, Cap performs his string music in the paint, but these Minnesota trees make for a dense forest. Also underwhelming: Mikal Bridges, who threw the ball at the basket just once in his 11 minutes before intermission. It’s sort of wild that the Knicks posted 65 first-half points despite getting only nine points from their starting backcourt.Also weird: Rudy Gobert had just five points and one rebound in his first 15 minutes. In fact, the Wolves’ starting frontcourt of McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga, and Gobert combined for two rebounds. Believe it, Ripley! They weren’t the only stinkers on the home team. Ball, Kuminga, and Ayo Dosunmu combined to shoot 4-of-17 through the half. Minnesota shot a respectable 44% overall and 39% from three, but outside of McDaniels, nobody found much rhythm. With the Knicks shooting a blistering 57% from the field and an eye-popping 63% from deep (10-of-16), the good guys were ahead 65-50 at intermission.In the third quarter, Brunson shouldered the load, scoring 14 points in the period, and Bridges showed up to sink a three and commit two thefts. Towns continued to crash the glass but cooled off somewhat offensively, as did OG. For the home team, Kuminga poured in 14 points, making two three-pointers while blocking three shots. The Wolves couldn’t put together a sustained run, though. Trailing 83-66 with around 3:30 left, they outscored our heroes 12-7, cutting the score to 90-78 at the break.To start the final frame, Kolek converted a four-point play to give the guests a 16-point lead. But we never thought the Furballs would roll over and die—and no, they didn’t. As New York’s offense stalled (e.g., Towns missed four of five, which he redeemed with three stuffs), McDaniels, Trey Lyles, and the Wolves chipped away at the lead. After New York went ahead 97-85 with 7:56 remaining, Minnesota scored eight unanswered points, including a McDaniels three and a Ball pull-up triple, to cut the lead to four. The Knicks went nearly four minutes without scoring, prompting a timeout and the return of Bridges and Anunoby.What makes tonight’s win most stunning is that New York managed to achieve it despite going scoreless over the final 3:26. During that grisly stretch, KAT copped a flopping tech, Gobert slammed an alley-oop, and Ayo buried a three, bringing the Timberwolves within three with 2:34 left. Brunson missed a pull-up jumper, New York committed a shot-clock violation, Towns was called for an offensive foul with 1:04 left, and Bridges missed a turnaround jumper with 23 seconds remaining.The hosts had plenty of chances to tie or steal the lead but couldn’t capitalize. Ball bricked two shots in the final 1:39; Dosunmu whiffed a bunny; and Bridges blocked Gobert’s putback attempt with 44 seconds left—arguably the biggest defensive play of the game. Ball blanked on a potential tying longball with 10 seconds remaining, and Kuminga collected the rebound but threw the ball away, with Landry Shamet securing the steal to end Minnesota’s night. For those keeping track at home, the Timberwolves missed their final six field-goal attempts and committed five turnovers over the last five minutes. That’s a lot of ugly basketball to taint what was otherwise a quite pleasant viewing experience. But a win’s a win! And this one came over a very worthy opponent.The Knicks host the Blazers on Saturday. Mo is sewing arms and legs onto your recap. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”Evasive and irregular turns“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

item.title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert

item.content:encoded: In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s going to be bittersweet’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: Revenge game for KAT today?I don’t think so, but who knows.Here’s the latest before visiting the Wolves in still-not-overly-cold Minnesota.On Rick Brunson’s decision to bring Jose Alvarado into the game against Toronto:“Just a great call. Rick Brunson made the call of throwing Jose in to see if he can give us a spark. So, just a heckuva call by Rick Brunson and just a fantastic job by Jose producing on both sides of the ball when his name was called.”On Karl-Anthony Towns improving his passing decisions and avoiding risks:“It’s a fine balance because he’s capable of making some beautiful passes in tight windows so you want to let him be him. But I thought earlier in the year — and we talked to him about it, and said it a couple times — he was trying to make the home-run pass a little too much.“And he’s gotten to a point where he’s mixing it up now. We’re going to trust him because he’s obviously done it for many years now with good results. We’ll lean on him quite a bit in that regard but if we turn the ball over too much, we’ll let him know.”On Towns’ basketball intelligence and ability to read the game:“KAT’s got tremendous feel. He’s a smart, smart dude when it comes to a lot of things, but especially when it comes to the game of basketball.”On Towns’ coachability and the impact of assistant coaches Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman:“It’s easy to see where he is, because everything we’ve asked him to do, he’s tried to do. So, you’re extremely coachable. You got a great feel. And you got two guys in (assistant coaches) Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman that are teaching you the game defensively at a really high level, and you’re starting to see the results of it.”On the Knicks’ execution and contributions throughout the roster against Toronto:“Our execution was at an extremely high level. We had a lot of guys contribute in a lot of ways tonight.”On the Knicks early-season woes:“It’s still a work in progress.”On why the NBA must continue penalizing dangerous closeouts and landing-space violations after Brunson’s injury scare:“They got to keep track of it because it’s going to happen. Everybody wants to try to block [Brunson’s] shot and every other guy’s shot. Some guys go forward too much and, if they do, there’s got to be a heavy penalty. Because if there’s no heavy penalty, then guys won’t be conscious of it. They’ll just keep sliding underneath guys.”On why his shooting technique sometimes exposes him to dangerous situations:“I fade a little bit. Taller guys are usually guarding me, so I got to be able to fade a little bit. Sometimes they’re not jumping straight up. They’re jumping towards me. It happens.”On prioritizing getting buckets over worrying about landing on a defender’s foot:“I’m not worried about falling on his foot. I’m more worried about if he’s close enough to block it. If he is too close, I probably won’t shoot it. If he’s not, ball is going up.”On the Knicks rediscovering their preferred style of play against Toronto:“We just played to the best of our abilities. I know the early season hasn’t looked like it, but that’s how we’re most comfortable.”On the disappointment of not winning a championship during his nine seasons in Minnesota:“I wanted to win one there. I didn’t accomplish that. But it was great to have those moments, to bring Minnesota back to the playoffs and be able to do a lot of things.”On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion with the Knicks:“It’s going to be bittersweet. I’m just happy that I have such amazing fans and had such an amazing time in Minnesota. I love it to death. I love that place so it’s going to be cool to go back.”On becoming a minority owner of Napoli’s basketball team:“Napoli is a great underdog story and reminds me of what we have built with the Knicks in many ways. It is a project built around hard work, big dreams and the incredible passion Napoli fans have for their team. I’ve been coming to Naples and the Amalfi Coast for years, and I know what a fan base like this can mean to a team. Seeing this club already making noise in the EuroCup tells you where it’s headed.“Matt Rizzetta and the team at Underdog Global Partners have high ambitions with a real plan for where this club is going. The Napoli journey is still very much in the first quarter, so I am excited to be a part of building this into something truly special in the years ahead.”On Instagram after being demoted from starting center to the second unit:“Nobody gone save me, gotta save my damn self.”

item.title: Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, Paul Seixas among cycling stars set for audience with Pope Leo XIV
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: A host of representatives from the cycling world, including Demi Vollering, Eddy Merckx, and Paul Seixas, will attend an audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican next week.UCI President David Lappartient described the November 23 event as "an opportunity to strengthen cycling's commitment, as a sport, to promoting peace and intercultural dialogue among peoples."Past and present Grand Tour champions are among a group of over 100 "distinguished guests" attending, in addition to organisers of all men's and women's Grand Tours and other races, and representatives from various cycling federations.Vollering, Merckx, and Seixas will be joined by a host of current and former road riders, including Bernard Hinault, Annemiek van Vleuten, Greg LeMond, Elisa Longo Borghini, Francesco Moser, Miguel Indurain, Jeannie Longo, Vincenzo Nibali, Chris Froome, and Mark Cavendish.Multiple para-cycling world champion Ricardo Ten Argilés, multiple BMX world champion Mariana Pajón, and Ukrainian cyclist Anna Kolyzhuk, who suffered a serious spinal injury in a crash during a race this year, will also attend.Ahead of the event, Lappartient "highlighted the longstanding historical roots between cycling and the Catholic Church, from races organised by parish communities and cycling teams inspired by Gospel values, to the various meetings with Popes throughout the 20th century and the recent passage of the Giro d’Italia through the Vatican during the 2025 Jubilee."The event will see Pope Leo XIV take an audience with the riders before the UCI symbolically donates several bicycles to Caritas Rome, a charitable organisation founded by the Episcopal Conference of Italy.The audience isn't the first time the Pope and the cycling world have come together. In 2025, the Pope blessed the peloton ahead of the final stage of the Giro d'Italia, which started in the Vatican. The stage was dedicated to Pope Francis, who died in April.Several other Popes have addressed the Giro in the past, including Pope Paul VI in 1964 and Pope John Paul II in 2000. Pope John Paul II also offered his support to the Amore e Vita cycling team in the 1990s and 2000s.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Plus, the Cyclingnews app means you can stay up-to-date wherever you go!

item.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
item.author: Kaamil Ahmed in The Hague and Yassin Abdumonab in Cox's Bazar
item.content:encoded: Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the worldThere were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Should Manchester United fans be hoping for relegation?’ Will Unwin answered your questions
item.author: Will Unwin and Guardian moderators
item.content:encoded: As Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge at Anfield, the Guardian’s Will Unwin answered your questions on Manchester United’s new head coach, the boardroom, the academy and whether Frank Ilett will ever get a haircut. Every few months there is the report of a new “wonderkid” being signed: a South American full-back, a Scandinavian midfielder, a flying winger etc. But then they never seem to make the squad, let alone the first team. The same for our academy, which wins trophies regularly. Are there real prospects who could supplement or even improve the team? Is it too difficult to introduce them into Premier League games? Are they just investments for future sell-on? And why did JJ Gabriel leave?The simple answer for many, and we can take the Paraguayan left-back Diego León as our example here, is that they are plainly not good enough and signing them has been poor . Some will take time, Sekou Kone was brought in from Mali and is out on loan at Lausanne to gain experience. Developing footballers is not an exact science and bringing them in from all around the world is a complex process to begin with. It is reliant on human factors outside football, of whether they can quickly adapt to life in a new country before even thinking about what they do on the pitch. Continue reading...

item.title: Black Friday Garmin deals - Big discounts on computers, watches and hardware
item.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
item.content:encoded: Garmin products are some of the most popular items on sale during the Black Friday sales event. Garmin bike computers, smartwatches, lights, trainers and other hardware are often discounted, and the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales are often a good time to bag yourself a new piece of tech.Amazon, Garmin and Sigma Sports in the UK all have a host of discounted Garmin hardware already, with some very good prices for computers and watches. Let's kick off with the Forerunner 265? Want a quality smartwatch without going crazy on the price? This is it. Currently at its lowest-ever price, the 265 will cover all of your running needs. You can also use Spotify to take care of your music, as well as just using it as a cool everyday watch. View DealThe popular Forerunner 970 smartwatch is 13% off in three different colours. This premium running- and triathlon-focused smartwatch is geared to help you run and also provides HRV status and sleep metrics. This bundle deal from Garmin also comes with a Power Bank included to help with charging when needed.View DealThe fēnix 8 is 25% off already; this is the cheapest it has ever been on Amazon. There are also five versions to choose from in the 47mm face size variant. The Edge Explore 3 may have arrived, but the Explore 2 is still available and is a good option for riders prioritising navigation features without a lot of other bells and whistles. The Edge 540 is 14% off right now, though it was available for $244 last November. This is a good unit for all-around riding; keep watching to see if the price drops a little more. View DealThe Edge 840 is at its lowest price in 30 days on Amazon right now, though it has been on sale for less cash this year. Officially, this unit has been superceded by the 850, but it's still a very capable unit with a touchscreen. View DealThe Edge 550 is on sale right now with a healthy 20% off. This is a mighty computer, but we felt the lack of a touchscreen limited it slightly. If you are happy with buttons, take a look. The Edge 850 is also on sale, discounted by 17%. In essence, this is the 550 with a touchscreen. It's a slightly bigger unit with a touchscreen, a built-in speaker and all the usual Garmin training and fitness tools. View DealThe Edge 1040 Solar doesn't show a discount on Amazon right now, but it's $50 cheaper from the Garmin Amazon store than it is on their website sale right now, so I'm including the deal for you. If you want some Solar charging tech in a big unit this is a good unit. View DealThe Garmin Edge 1050 is a top-tier Garmin unit and is arguably still worth buying over the recently launched and more expensive Edge 1060. $100 off, this unit is a monster, with a brilliant, clear display and fast touchscreen. This unit pairs a rear light with a Bluetooth radar to help you monitor upcoming vehicles from up to 153 yards away. If you want a built-in camera too, scroll down. View DealThe Varia RCT715 is on sale in the US at 25% off. This unit brings together a camera, taillight and radar to help keep you safer on the bike. It Bluetooth-pairs with your head unit so you can view radar alerts.The Garmin Varia Vue is 27% off if you want to invest in front and rear Varia units. This camera/light pairs a 600-lumen front light with a 4K camera to capture your rides. Tip: You will need a Micro SD card for the unit too. View DealThe Flux 2 is discounted on the Garmin website; it's a solid smart trainer that prioritises low noise and is accurate within 2.5%. The trainer can connect with all the usual indoor training apps, so you can have a solid winter of riding. View DealThe Tacx Neo 2T with Zwift Cog and Click is 18% off right now. This top-level trainer comes with Zwift's Cog and Click sprocket pre-installed, plus clip-on virtual shifters, so you can use it easily with any bike. It also works without power in standalone mode, which is useful for races, events, or outdoor riding.View DealWant to go the whole hog with a premium smart bike? Th Neo Bike Plus has a 10% discount. This is a fully adjustable smart bike that aims to offer the ultimate immersion indoors. The trainer vibrates and simulates road surfaces; dynamic inertia tech makes it feel like an outdoor ride, and the built-in fans mimic wind and keep you cool. View DealGarmin's latest RS210 power meter pedals are on sale. This deal is for the RS210 dual-sided SPD SL option which gained recharging capability over the previous units battery powered tech. SPD and SPD-SL pedal bodies can be switched onto the axles, and the pedals are accurate to within +/-1%. View DealThe Forerunner 55 is a nice entry point into the world of smartwatches and has a healthy discount in the black colour. This watch will suit runners, but will suit anyone just wanting a Garmin smartwatch with its two-week battery life. View DealThis early BF deal sees the fēnix 8 drop to its lowest ever price on Amazon in the 47 mm/slate grey version. The fēnix 8 is a top-level smartwatch with voice control and contactless payment tech. Its AMOLED screen is punchy and vivid, yet you still get up to 29 days of battery life in smartwatch mode. View DealThe Garmin Varia RCT715 is at 15% on Amazon, the same as Sigma and the Garmin sale. The RCT715 is a light, camera and rear radar in one and has daylight visibility up to a mile. The Edge Explore 2 is a more basic unit that prioritises mapping and navigation. It doesn't have as many bells and whistles, but if that's all you need, it's a solid buy.This is a really good price for the Garmin Edge 540. A solid little computer that's packed with a load of features. It doesn't have a touchscreen, so consider this point if it's a deal-breaker for you. The Edge 840 unit is just over 20% off and is available for under £300. This is a solid operator, but the Edge 850 which got an upgraded colour touschcreen is also on sale below. View DealHere's the solar-charging version of the Edge 840, also on sale with 25% off. If you live somewhere with lots of sunshine, this will be worth a look. I didn't find the solar tech too useful in the UK. The Garmin Edge 850 is also discounted by just under 20% in the Sigma sale. This unit has a colour touchscreen and has lots of advanced training features.View DealThis is a big saving on the Edge 1040 Solar, with over 25% off. In bright sunlight, we found it could go weeks without charging. Making it ideal for long rides or touring. Garmin's flagship model until the recent launch of the 1060, the 1050 is a powerhouse, with a built-in bell and contactless pay technology. It's packed with features; do you need them all? Our other Black Friday 2026 roundups👕 : With 25% off sitewide, we've rounded up our favourite items from the British brand.💾 : A roundup of our favourite deals on Wahoo tech, such as smart trainers and bike computers, from Wahoo's own website and beyond.
